title: QCon San Francisco 2026: How to Kill the Code Review
gist: At QCon San Francisco 2026, Aviator CEO Ankit Jain (flagging his commercial conflict) argued line-by-line code review is already effectively dead under AI-generated PR volume — most PRs merge without human review and reviews have become 'rubber stamping' — and proposed replacing it with six layers (Argue, Capture, Codify, Prove, Debate, Own) built on invariants and evidence. His own team reports 4x PR throughput with ~40% fewer reverts, while security, auth and billing still get line-by-line review.

themes.theme: Code review was never about bugs

insights.claim: A 2013 Microsoft study found 44% of reviewers cited defect-finding as their motivation but only 14% of review comments concerned defects, and a 2018 Google study of more than nine million reviews found nearly the same split.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Undermines the bug-catching rationale for human review, weakening resistance to automating or removing it.
insights.locator: He began with the data that unseated his original framing.

insights.claim: Ankit Jain argues code review's real function was knowledge sharing, so AI that makes writing code cheap leaves the cost of understanding unchanged, citing Addy Osmani.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: The bottleneck in AI-assisted development shifts to comprehension — tooling that conveys intent and understanding is the opportunity.
insights.quote: We made writing cheap, and understanding stayed exactly as expensive as it has always been.
insights.locator: Code review was never really about bugs

themes.theme: Review theater under AI PR volume

insights.claim: A September Faros study of more than 4,000 teams found over 75% of PRs now merge without any human review, average PR size has grown, and redo work is up 67% year over year.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Rising rework alongside unreviewed merges signals a quality gap that AI code-verification and review vendors can target.
insights.locator: A September Faros study of more than 4,000 teams

insights.claim: Review quality drops sharply beyond 400 lines, yet the median pull request today is 640 lines, meaning typical AI-era PRs exceed the size humans can review effectively.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Human review capacity is structurally outpaced by AI code volume — demand for automated verification grows.
insights.locator: Earlier research showed review quality drops sharply past 400 lines

insights.claim: Ankit Jain describes current practice as 'review theater': agents write code, another AI reviews it, agents revise, and humans skim and merge — reviews still happen but are rubber-stamped.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: AI-reviewing-AI loops without human understanding create latent risk; watch for outages and governance products addressing this.
insights.quote: We are reviewing the code, but we are rubber stamping it,
insights.locator: Earlier research showed review quality drops sharply past 400 lines

insights.claim: A Reddit post by an experienced developer refusing to review AI-generated pull requests collected over 1,900 upvotes, indicating developer backlash against reviewing AI-written code.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Developer fatigue with AI PR review is a sentiment signal for adoption friction and for tools that reduce review burden.
insights.locator: pointing to a Reddit post from an experienced developer

insights.claim: Ankit Jain predicts the next question for engineering teams is not whether to do line-by-line review — which he says is already quietly dead on most teams — but how long until developers stop reading the code at all.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: If code reading declines, value shifts to specification, verification and evidence tooling around AI-generated code.
insights.quote: how long until we stop reading the code?
insights.locator: Closing the Engineering the Developer Experience track

insights.claim: Jain proposes replacing a single code review with six layers — Argue (agents debate a change locally before the PR exists), Capture (intent and acceptance criteria attached to the PR), Codify (repeated comments become invariants), Prove (evidence), Debate (humans debate decisions, not diffs) and Own (teams own the rules).
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: A blueprint for the post-review SDLC; tooling vendors that implement these layers (including Aviator) stand to benefit.
insights.locator: To replace a single review, Jain proposed six layers

insights.claim: Repeated review comments should be converted into invariants — standing rules with scope, provenance, a verification method and a team owner; Aviator mined 11,000 of its own review comments to produce 64 invariants.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Shows review knowledge compresses heavily (~170 comments per rule), making codified rule engines a plausible product category.

insights.claim: Because the same agent that wrote the code likely also wrote its unit tests, green test checks should be replaced by evidence such as screenshots, DOM snapshots, recorded requests, latencies and database logs.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Passing CI is a weaker quality signal for agent-written code; evidence-capture and runtime-verification tooling gains relevance.

insights.claim: Eight months after his March 2026 Latent Space essay proposing a five-layer trust model to replace reviews, Jain said its mechanics held up but it entirely missed human judgment, leading to the revised six-layer model.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Even automation advocates are re-inserting human judgment — full removal of humans from the loop is not the consensus endpoint.
insights.locator: The talk revisited an essay he wrote for Latent Space

insights.claim: Ankit Jain reported his nine-engineer team at Aviator merges four times as many PRs as a year ago while still approving every one, and reverts have dropped around 40%.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: A vendor-reported proof point (author flagged conflict of interest) that rule/evidence-based workflows can raise throughput and quality together.
insights.locator: Jain reported his nine-engineer team now merges four times the PRs

insights.claim: At Aviator a change passed every automated filter yet caused an 18-minute outage from an unindexed query, and the post-mortem asked which rule was missing rather than who approved it.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Automated gates still leak production incidents; accountability shifts from individuals to rule coverage.

insights.claim: Even under Jain's post-review model, critical areas such as security, authentication and billing still receive line-by-line human review.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Human code review persists for high-risk domains, sustaining demand for security-focused review tools.
insights.locator: Critical areas such as security, authentication and billing

insights.claim: Ankit Jain, co-founder and CEO of Aviator, openly flagged that his company sells a solution to the problem he describes and asked the audience to be suspicious of him.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Discount the claims as vendor positioning; the third-party data (Microsoft, Google, Faros) is the more neutral evidence.
insights.locator: He also flagged his conflict of interest up front
